_note: Reference library. mcl = EPA enforceable limit (or action level / secondary standard). health_guideline = stricter public-health goal (EWG / state / MCLG) where it meaningfully differs. removed_by: ro | whole_home | both.

nitrate.name: Nitrate
nitrate.health_effects: High nitrate is especially dangerous for infants under 6 months, causing 'blue baby syndrome' (methemoglobinemia) where blood can't carry oxygen. Linked in studies to certain cancers and thyroid effects in adults.
nitrate.sources: Fertilizer and agricultural runoff, septic systems, manure — common in Minnesota's farm-influenced groundwater.

pfas.name: PFAS (PFOA / PFOS – “Forever Chemicals”)
pfas.health_effects: PFAS build up in the body and don't break down. Linked to kidney and testicular cancer, thyroid disease, high cholesterol, immune suppression, and developmental effects in children. The EPA set a near-zero health goal for PFOA and PFOS.
pfas.sources: Industrial discharge, firefighting foam, and the 3M manufacturing legacy that contaminated East Metro groundwater (Washington & Dakota counties).

arsenic.name: Arsenic
arsenic.health_effects: A known human carcinogen. Long-term exposure is linked to bladder, lung and skin cancers, skin damage, and cardiovascular disease. Minnesota has naturally elevated arsenic in many groundwater wells.
arsenic.sources: Naturally occurring in Minnesota bedrock and glacial aquifers.

lead.name: Lead
lead.health_effects: There is no safe level of lead. It damages the developing brain and nervous system in children, lowering IQ and attention. In adults it raises blood pressure and harms kidneys. Leaches from old service lines and home plumbing — common in older Minneapolis and Saint Paul homes.
lead.sources: Corrosion of lead service lines, solder, and brass fixtures — the lead is picked up after water leaves the treatment plant.

manganese.name: Manganese
manganese.mcl_label: MN health guidance 100 ppb (50 ppb for infants)
manganese.health_effects: The Minnesota Department of Health warns that high manganese can affect memory, attention and motor skills — with infants and children most at risk. It also stains laundry and fixtures brownish-black.
manganese.sources: Naturally occurring in Minnesota groundwater — very common in metro-area wells.
manganese.aesthetic: Black/brown staining on fixtures and laundry; bitter metallic taste.

iron.name: Iron
iron.health_effects: Not a major health risk, but a constant nuisance.
iron.sources: Naturally dissolved from Minnesota soil and rock into groundwater.
iron.aesthetic: Rusty orange/red staining on sinks, tubs, toilets and laundry; metallic taste; clogs fixtures and appliances.

chromium6.name: Chromium-6 (Hexavalent Chromium)
chromium6.health_effects: The 'Erin Brockovich' chemical — a likely human carcinogen when ingested. California's public-health goal is 5,000x stricter than the federal total-chromium limit.

tthm.name: Total Trihalomethanes (TTHMs)
tthm.health_effects: Disinfection byproducts formed when chlorine reacts with organic matter. Long-term exposure is associated with increased cancer risk and effects on pregnancy. More common in surface-water systems like Minneapolis and Saint Paul.
tthm.sources: Byproduct of chlorine disinfection at the treatment plant.

haa5.name: Haloacetic Acids (HAA5)
haa5.health_effects: A second family of disinfection byproducts linked to cancer risk over a lifetime of exposure.

fluoride.name: Fluoride
fluoride.health_effects: Added to Minnesota public water for dental health. Some homeowners prefer to reduce it for drinking water; reverse osmosis does so effectively.

chloride.name: Chloride
chloride.health_effects: Not a direct health risk at typical levels, but chloride from road salt is steadily rising across Twin Cities water and is impossible to remove at the city plant.
chloride.sources: Winter road salt and water-softener salt discharge — a documented and growing Twin Cities problem.
chloride.aesthetic: Salty taste; corrodes plumbing at high levels.

sodium.name: Sodium
sodium.health_effects: A concern for those on low-sodium diets or with high blood pressure. Traditional salt-based softening adds sodium — which is exactly why pairing softening with reverse osmosis for drinking water matters.
sodium.sources: Road salt, natural minerals, and salt-based softeners.

sulfate.name: Sulfate
sulfate.health_effects: High levels can have a laxative effect, especially on visitors and infants not used to it.
sulfate.aesthetic: Bitter taste; rotten-egg odor when combined with sulfur bacteria.

radium.name: Radium (226 + 228)
radium.health_effects: A naturally radioactive element linked to increased cancer risk over long-term exposure. Found in some deep Minnesota wells.
radium.sources: Natural radioactive decay in deep aquifers.

chlorine.name: Chlorine / Chloramine
chlorine.health_effects: Necessary to keep city water safe in the pipes, but creates the disinfection byproducts above and dries out skin and hair.
chlorine.sources: Added at the treatment plant to disinfect.
chlorine.aesthetic: 'Pool water' taste and smell; dry skin and hair; dulls laundry.

tds.name: Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
tds.health_effects: The total of all dissolved minerals, salts and metals in your water. Not a single toxin, but a good overall gauge — higher TDS means more 'stuff' in your water affecting taste and leaving spots and scale.
tds.sources: Combined minerals, salts, metals and other dissolved material.
tds.aesthetic: Spotty dishes, scale buildup, flat or mineral taste.

coliform.name: Coliform / E. coli Bacteria
coliform.health_effects: Indicates possible contamination by disease-causing organisms. A risk mainly for private wells and older systems.
coliform.sources: Surface water intrusion, septic systems, well-cap failures.
